question: Is there a person (pudgala) that is neither the same as nor different from the aggregates?

sides.position: There is a person, real, designated in dependence on the internal, appropriated, present aggregates — neither identical with them nor different, as fire is designated in dependence on fuel; it is inexpressible, the fifth kind of knowable; it bears the burden of the aggregates and transmigrates.
arguments: The sūtras speak of 'one person born in the world for the welfare of many' and of the burden-bearer (Bhārahāra-sūtra).
Without a person, karma and its result, memory, and rebirth have no bearer.
Fire is neither other than fuel (else fuel would not be hot) nor the same (else burned would be burner).

sides.position: There is no person apart from the series of aggregates; 'self' and 'person' are designations of that series. A person that is neither real nor a designation is incoherent; the five-knowables list cannot even be stated; the burden-bearer is the earlier aggregates.
arguments: If the person were a substance it would be other than the aggregates, with a cause, or unconditioned — the outsiders' view.
If it is designated, it is designated like milk, i.e. on the aggregates only.
No liberation for those who imagine a self as a separate entity.

sides.position: There is no self; only aggregates conditioned by defilements and karma go from life to life through the intermediate existence, like a flame.
The person is not found as a real and ultimate fact (saccikaṭṭha-paramattha).
arguments: The Puggalavādin cannot say the person is found in the same way as real ultimate facts are.

historical_debates.name: Kathāvatthu 1.1 (the Puggalakathā)
historical_debates.date: tradition: Third Council at Pāṭaliputra under Aśoka
historical_debates.accounts: Kathāvatthu and its commentary (opponents named as Vajjiputtakas and Sammitiyas)

historical_debates.name: Abhidharmakośabhāṣya ch. 9
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Vasubandhu: refuted; the Saṃmitīya nevertheless flourished in the 7th c. (Xuanzang, Yijing)

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: both sides accept that the person is spoken of in dependence on the aggregates, but disagree whether it is anything beyond a designation.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Pudgalavādins insisted the person is real and neither the same as nor different from the aggregates; the Theravāda (Kathāvatthu), the Sarvāstivāda and Vasubandhu insist no person exists as a real and ultimate fact. Both reject a reconciliation that makes their position merely verbal.

candidate_readings: P1-level: 'person' is valid at the conventional level for both; the dispute concerns only its ultimate status — rejected by the Pudgalavādins, who deny the person is a mere designation.
P2-standpoint: the 'inexpressible' as a standpoint neither of identity nor of difference, comparable to other tetralemma answers — rejected by Vasubandhu as a fifth category unknown to the Buddha.
P5-neyartha: sūtras speaking of 'a person' (the burden-bearer) are provisional — accepted by the Sarvāstivāda and Theravāda, rejected by the Pudgalavāda.
notes: Related to the registry dispute dsp:is-there-a-self (U50), which concerns the non-Buddhist self; Śāntarakṣita's Tattvasaṃgraha also examines the Vātsīputrīya self (low confidence on the chapter). Related dispute from the Theravāda side: dsp:kv-puggala (U37, the Kathāvatthu debate); this entry records the cross-school debate — candidate for dedupe/merge at synthesis.

question: Do past and future dharmas exist?

sides.position: Yes: all dharmas exist in all three times as real entities; the times are distinguished by activity (kāritra).
arguments: The Buddha taught that past and future matter is to be regarded as not self — so it exists.
Consciousness arises from two (faculty and object); a consciousness of the past needs an existent object.
Past karma yields its result, so it exists.
The four masters explain the distinction of the times; Vasumitra's 'state' is best.

sides.position: No: only the present exists; the conditioned 'arises having not been, and having been ceases'; results arise from the transformed series preceded by the karma.
arguments: A remembered past thing is not seen as existing now.
If past and future existed like the present, they would be present.
If the result already exists, what does karma do?

sides.position: Partly: past karma that has not yet given its fruit exists; the rest of the past and the future do not (the Vibhajyavāda position).
No: 'everything exists' is refuted.
No: past and future have no real existence (Vasumitra).

historical_debates.name: Saṅghabhadra against Vasubandhu
historical_debates.accounts: Nyāyānusāra; Xuanzang's account of the challenge that never took place
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Vaibhāṣika: the Kośa refuted; Sautrāntika and later tradition: the bhāṣya's criticisms stand

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Sarvāstivāda affirms the real existence of past and future dharmas; the Sautrāntika, Mahāsāṃghika, Mahīśāsaka and Theravāda deny it, the Kāśyapīya partly.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Vaibhāṣikas hold that denial of past and future makes karma, memory and cognition of the past impossible; the Sautrāntikas hold that affirming them makes everything eternal and the present unintelligible ('deep indeed is the nature of dharmas' is not an answer).

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Vaibhāṣika speaks of a dharma's own-nature (substance, dravyārthika) which does not change, the Sautrāntika of its activity and moment (mode, paryāyārthika); the Vaibhāṣika itself distinguishes the times only by activity — rejected by both, since each affirms or denies real existence, not a standpoint.
Soteriological reading: both explain how past karma bears fruit and how past defilements can be known and abandoned — by existence (Vaibhāṣika) or by the transformed series (Sautrāntika).
notes: Related dispute from the Theravāda side: dsp:kv-sabbam-atthi (U37, the Kathāvatthu debate); this entry records the cross-school debate — candidate for dedupe/merge at synthesis.

question: Is there an intermediate existence (antarābhava) between death and rebirth?

sides.position: Yes: existence continues without interruption like the series of a grain; the gandharva at conception, the non-returner who attains nirvāṇa 'in between', and the sūtra of the destinies prove it; the intermediate being has the form of its next life and feeds on smells.
Yes (Kathāvatthu commentary on Kv 8.2 names the Pubbaseliyas and Sammitiyas).
No: an intermediate existence is none of the three kinds of existence; rebirth follows death immediately.
No (Vasumitra).
No (Vasumitra).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: a disagreement about what happens between death and rebirth.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each side reads the same sūtra passages as definitive for its own view.

candidate_readings: Scriptural reading: the sūtra terms (gandharva, antarāparinirvāyin) read literally (Sarvāstivāda) or otherwise (Theravāda: one who attains nirvāṇa in the first half of life) — no principle settles which is definitive (P5-neyartha contested).
notes: Related dispute from the Theravāda side: dsp:kv-antarabhava (U37, the Kathāvatthu debate); this entry records the cross-school debate — candidate for dedupe/merge at synthesis.

question: Can an arhat fall back from arhatship?

sides.position: Yes: of six kinds of arhat, five ('liberated by occasion') can fall back from the fruit; the unshakeable cannot; stream-enterers cannot fall back; one fallen does not die before regaining it.
Yes (Kathāvatthu commentary on Kv 1.2 names Sammitiyas, Vajjiputtakas, Sabbatthivādins and some Mahāsaṅghikas).
No: defilements abandoned by seeing do not return, and there is no falling back from arhatship either; what is lost is only the enjoyment of attainments.
No: the arahant does not fall away (Kv 1.2).
Arhats cannot fall back; stream-enterers can (Vasumitra).

reconciliation.explanation: All sides agree that the unshakeable (akopya) arhat and the 'falling back from enjoyment' of attainments are not in question; the remaining disagreement is whether the fruit itself can be lost.
reconciliation.detail: The Kośa's threefold falling back (from what is obtained, not obtained, enjoyment) lets the Sautrāntika accept loss of enjoyment while denying loss of the fruit.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Sarvāstivāda insists five kinds of arhat lose the fruit itself (6.58 'phalād dhāniḥ'); the Theravāda denies it; neither accepts that the difference is merely one of standpoint.

notes: Related dispute from the Theravāda side: dsp:kv-arahant-falling-away (U37, the Kathāvatthu debate); this entry records the cross-school debate — candidate for dedupe/merge at synthesis.

question: Does the arhat still have imperfections (the five points of Mahādeva)?

sides.position: Yes (as reported by opponents): an arhat can be tempted by others to an impure emission, still has non-knowing and doubt, is brought to understanding by others, and the path arises with an utterance.
arguments: Reported only by the Sarvāstivāda and Theravāda sources.

sides.position: Yes (Kathāvatthu commentary on Kv 2.1–2.6 names the Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas).
No: these are heresies; Mahādeva was a sinner who caused the schism (Vibhāṣā). Yet the Kośa itself holds that only the Buddha has destroyed non-defiled ignorance.
No: each of the points is refuted.

historical_debates.name: The first schism at Pāṭaliputra
historical_debates.date: tradition: over a century after the parinirvāṇa, under Aśoka
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Sarvāstivāda: the majority (Mahāsāṃghika) followed Mahādeva, the elders withdrew

reconciliation.explanation: Points two and three (non-knowing, doubt) can be read as non-defiled ignorance and uncertainty about matters outside liberation, which the Sarvāstivāda itself attributes to arhats (AK 1.1 bhāṣya); the other points remain not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.detail: Only the Buddha has destroyed darkness 'in every way' (AK 1.1), i.e. including non-defiled ignorance.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Vibhāṣā presents all five as heresy and would not accept that Mahādeva meant non-defiled ignorance; the Mahāsāṃghika's own wording is lost.

notes: Related dispute from the Theravāda side: dsp:kv-arahant-imperfections (U37, the Kathāvatthu debate); this entry records the cross-school debate — candidate for dedupe/merge at synthesis.

question: Are the four truths realized gradually (in successive moments) or in a single moment?

sides.position: Gradually: sixteen moments of acceptance and knowledge, dharma- and subsequent knowledge for each truth; fifteen are the path of seeing.
In one moment: path-knowledge penetrates the four truths simultaneously (Theravāda commentarial position; low confidence on the canonical Kathāvatthu reference).
In one moment (ascribed to the Mahāsāṃghika side in doxographic summaries; low confidence).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the realization of the four truths as sixteen successive moments or as one.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each side holds its count of moments to be the actual structure of the path.

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the sixteen moments describe the phases of one path-event from the side of its objects (the truths and realms), the single moment from the side of its function (abandonment) — rejected by the Vaibhāṣika, for whom the moments are distinct dharmas.
P4-stage: gradual in the preparatory roots of penetration, single in the path itself.
notes: Distinct from the registry debate dsp:sudden-or-gradual (Chan/Samye), which concerns awakening and practice, not the moments of the path of seeing. Related dispute from the Theravāda side: dsp:kv-gradual-penetration (U37, the Kathāvatthu debate); this entry records the cross-school debate — candidate for dedupe/merge at synthesis.

question: Is the Buddha's bodily existence supramundane, or human and impure (sāsrava)?

sides.position: Supramundane: the Buddha's conduct, merit, postures, body, robes and food are beyond the world; his human acts are only conformity to the world.
All Tathāgatas are supramundane and without outflows; body, power and life are limitless (Vasumitra).

The Buddha's physical body is the result of former karma and can be the object of others' defilements, hence with outflows; one takes refuge not in it but in the non-learner's dharmas; Buddhas differ in lifespan and stature.
The Buddha lived in the human world; it is wrong to deny it (against the Vetulyakas per the commentary).

reconciliation.explanation: Both sides place what is truly 'Buddha' in the pure qualities (dharmakāya / the supramundane) and treat his worldly appearance as conventional — the Lokottaravāda explicitly as skilful conformity (lokānuvartanā).
reconciliation.detail: Whether the physical body itself is supramundane or sāsrava remains not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Lokottaravāda insists the body and bodily acts are themselves supramundane; the Theravāda and Sarvāstivāda insist the Buddha was born, lived and died as a human.

notes: Related dispute from the Theravāda side: dsp:kv-buddha-in-human-world (U37, the Kathāvatthu debate); this entry records the cross-school debate — candidate for dedupe/merge at synthesis.

question: What caused the first schism between the Sthaviras and the Mahāsāṃghikas?

sides.position: Laxity in discipline: the Vajjiputtakas' ten points were rejected at Vesālī; the defeated monks formed the Mahāsaṅgītika and altered the texts.
Doctrine: Mahādeva's five points lowering the arhat divided the Saṅgha under Aśoka.
Vinaya recension: an elder enlarged and rearranged the Vinaya; the great community kept the original.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the schools remember different causes for the first division of the Saṅgha.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each tradition presents its own side as the faithful one and the other as the innovators.

candidate_readings: Historical reading: several successive disputes (the ten points at Vaiśālī, the five points, Vinaya recension) each remembered by the side it justified — the traditions do not frame it so.
P2-standpoint: each account is true from the standpoint of its community's discipline — rejected by each, which regards the other side as having departed from the Dharma-Vinaya.

question: Is possession (prāpti) a real entity?

sides.position: Yes: a real dissociated force linking dharmas to a series; the state of an ordinary person is non-possession of the noble path.
No: 'possession' is the intact seed in the series; the ordinary person is the series in which the noble dharmas have not arisen.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Vaibhāṣika holds a real entity where the Sautrāntika sees a designation.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each side holds the other's account inadequate: the Vaibhāṣika that designations cannot do causal work, the Sautrāntika that the posited entities are unnecessary and unattested in the sūtras.

candidate_readings: P1-level: 'possession' as a valid conventional description of the seed-state — rejected by the Vaibhāṣika, who holds it a dravya.

question: Is unmanifest matter (avijñapti) a real entity?

sides.position: Yes: unmanifest matter carries vows and non-vows through time, even when mind is absent.
No: shape and avijñapti are not entities; the course of action is the transformation of the series produced by volition.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Vaibhāṣika holds a real entity where the Sautrāntika sees a designation.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each side holds the other's account inadequate: the Vaibhāṣika that designations cannot do causal work, the Sautrāntika that the posited entities are unnecessary and unattested in the sūtras.

candidate_readings: P1-level: 'unmanifest matter' as the conventional name for the karmic continuity — rejected by the Vaibhāṣika.

question: Are the unconditioned dharmas (space, the two cessations) real entities?

sides.position: Yes: three real, eternal unconditioned dharmas; nirvāṇa is cessation through discernment, a real disjunction.
No: all the unconditioned is unreal — space is absence of resistance, nirvāṇa the non-arising of further defilement and birth.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Vaibhāṣika holds a real entity where the Sautrāntika sees a designation.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each side holds the other's account inadequate: the Vaibhāṣika that designations cannot do causal work, the Sautrāntika that the posited entities are unnecessary and unattested in the sūtras.

candidate_readings: P1-level / apophatic reading: nirvāṇa described positively (as a dharma) or negatively (as absence) — the Vaibhāṣika insists on its reality, the Sautrāntika on its unreality.
notes: Related dispute from the Theravāda side: dsp:kv-unconditioned-dhammas (U37, the Kathāvatthu debate); this entry records the cross-school debate — candidate for dedupe/merge at synthesis.

question: Does the destruction of a conditioned thing have a cause?

sides.position: Impermanence is one of the four real characteristics that acts on each dharma; destruction is characterized, though things are momentary.
No: destruction is causeless and spontaneous; what arises perishes of itself; apparent destruction by fire is non-arising of a similar series.
Some formations are momentary, others endure for a time (Vasumitra).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Vaibhāṣika holds a real entity where the Sautrāntika sees a designation.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each side holds the other's account inadequate: the Vaibhāṣika that designations cannot do causal work, the Sautrāntika that the posited entities are unnecessary and unattested in the sūtras.

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the characteristic 'impermanence' names what the Sautrāntika calls the thing's own perishing — rejected by both as to the reality of the characteristic.

question: Are the Abhidharma treatises the word of the Buddha?

sides.position: Yes: the Buddha taught the Abhidharma scattered through his discourses; Kātyāyanīputra and others gathered it, as Dharmatrāta gathered the Udāna verses.
No: the treatises have known human authors; the 'Abhidharma basket' consists of particular sūtras such as the Arthaviniścaya.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: whether the Abhidharma treatises are the word of the Buddha.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Vaibhāṣika holds the treatises to be buddhavacana; the Sautrāntika holds only the sūtras are.

candidate_readings: P5-neyartha: both agree the characteristics of dharmas were taught by the Buddha; the disagreement concerns the authority of the compiled treatises.
notes: Related dispute from the Theravāda side: dsp:authority-of-abhidhamma (U37, the Kathāvatthu debate); this entry records the cross-school debate — candidate for dedupe/merge at synthesis.

question: Is the mind by nature luminous and only adventitiously defiled?

sides.position: Yes: the nature of mind is originally pure, defiled by adventitious defilements (Vasumitra).
Yes (as reported in the Vibhāṣā).
No: a mind with defilement is not pure; purity and defilement are successive states.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: whether the mind is by nature luminous.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Sarvāstivāda denies an 'original nature' of mind distinct from its momentary states.

candidate_readings: P1-level: luminous in its nature (ultimate), defiled in its occurrence (conventional) — rejected by the Sarvāstivāda, for which a defiled mind is not pure in any respect.
notes: Related dispute from the Theravāda side: dsp:luminous-citta-reading (U37, the Kathāvatthu debate); this entry records the cross-school debate — candidate for dedupe/merge at synthesis.

question: What sees — the eye, consciousness, or neither?

sides.position: The eye sees, as the support of consciousness, since forms behind a wall are not seen.
Neither: visual consciousness arises from eye and form; 'the eye sees' and 'consciousness cognizes' are conventions over a mere set of dharmas without activity.

reconciliation.explanation: The Sautrāntika itself accepts 'the eye sees' as a valid convention; disagreement remains on whether it is also true in the ultimate sense.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Vaibhāṣika holds that the eye really sees and would reject treating its thesis as merely conventional.

question: Does sense perception grasp the external object directly, or only its form (ākāra) in cognition?

sides.position: Directly: sense consciousness grasps a present, really existing object, without an image; consciousness always needs an existent object (the argument for three-time existence).

Through its form: cognition arises bearing the object's form; the external object, already past when cognition arises, is inferred (as summarized in later doxography; low confidence for the Indian sources).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: whether perception grasps its object directly or through the object's form in cognition.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Later doxography (Tibetan grub mtha') sharpens the positions beyond the Indian Abhidharma texts.

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint — rejected by both as to the structure of cognition.

question: Does a gift to the Buddha yield more merit than a gift to the Saṅgha?

sides.position: Yes: though included in the Saṅgha, the Buddha as a separate field yields greater fruit; offerings to stūpas bring great fruit (Vasumitra).
No: the Buddha is included in the Saṅgha, so a gift to the Saṅgha has great fruit (Vasumitra).
Merit depends on giver, thing and field; merit arises even at a stūpa where no one receives.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the relative merit of gifts to the Buddha and to the Saṅgha.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each school's Vinaya practice follows its view.

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Buddha as member of the Saṅgha (Mahīśāsaka) or as its unsurpassed field (Dharmaguptaka).
The Kośa's criterion: the field is distinguished by qualities; the highest gift is from the liberated to the liberated.

question: Can the full ordination of nuns be introduced in the Mūlasarvāstivāda (Tibetan) tradition?

sides.position: Only by a procedure valid under the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, which requires a quorum of bhikṣuṇīs of the same lineage; such a lineage is absent in Tibet (conservative view).
The Dharmaguptaka bhikṣuṇī lineage, living in East Asia, can supply the nuns' side of a dual ordination (reformist view).

historical_debates.name: International Congress on Buddhist Women's Role in the Saṅgha

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: whether and how full ordination of nuns can be conferred where the Mūlasarvāstivāda bhikṣuṇī lineage was never transmitted.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Many Tibetan Vinaya authorities hold that mixing Vinaya lineages or ordination by monks alone is not valid under the Mūlasarvāstivāda code.

candidate_readings: Vinaya reading: dual ordination with Dharmaguptaka bhikṣuṇīs and Mūlasarvāstivāda bhikṣus.
Vinaya reading: ordination by bhikṣus alone, as permitted at the order's beginning.
